I wrote `polyglot/main.rs`. It builds with both `rustc` and `g++ -x c++`, and both programs print the same results. I checked N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 10, 50, 90 and 150: for example, N = 0 gives 1, N = 10 gives 89 and N = 150 gives 16130531424904581415797907386349. I deleted the test binaries afterwards, so only `main.rs` is left in the folder.

**How it works:** the trick is that the two compilers treat comments differently.
- **Rust:** block comments can be nested, so the opening `/* /* */` is still an open comment when it reaches `#if 0`, and that comment closes on the next line. Rust then compiles the `fn main`. At the end, a line comment ending in `\` is just a comment to Rust, so the `/*` on the next line hides all of the C++ code until the final `*/`.
- **C++:** block comments don't nest, so `/* /* */` is one complete comment. `#if 0 … #endif` then skips the Rust code. In C++, a `//` comment ending in `\` carries on to the next line, which swallows the `/*` and `*/` that Rust needed.

**Numbers:** both versions use 128-bit integers, so results are exact up to about N = 184. Above that, the numbers wrap around silently, and both versions wrap the same way. If you leave out N or pass something that isn't a number, both print 1 (treated as N = 0). The C++ version converts the 128-bit value to text by hand, because `printf` can't print 128-bit integers.
